Some FHIR for Research workshops provide interactive [Jupyter notebooks](https://docs.jupyter.org/en/latest/#what-is-a-notebook). These notebooks make it easy to explore and run the provided Python code to develop a deeper technical understanding of the topic in question.

There are a number of ways to view or run Jupyter notebooks, and four are supported by this website:

1. **View the notebook on this website.** When you follow a link to a notebook on this website, you are viewing a rendered, static version of that notebook formatted for this website. This is the preferred option if you want to read through the code and surrounding narrative, but not run it.
2. **Download and run the notebook locally.** Click the !['Download notebook' badge](../images/badges/download_notebook.svg) button, and open it using [JupyterLab Desktop](#jupyterlab-desktop-recommended) or a local Python environment with Jupyter installed.
3. **View on nbviewer** to preview what you will see if you run the notebook locally. Click the !['View on nbviewer' badge](../images/badges/nbviewer.svg) to do this.
4. **Run in the cloud.** There are multiple options for this including [Binder](https://mybinder.org) and [Google Colab](#google-colab). Use the !['Open in Google Colab' badge](../images/badges/colab.svg) to open notebooks in Colab with one click.

## Running locally

There are a few different options for running Jupyter notebooks locally.

### JupyterLab Desktop (recommended)

[JupyterLab Desktop](https://github.com/jupyterlab/jupyterlab-desktop) provides a local notebook environment without requiring a separately managed Jupyter installation.

1. Install the appropriate [JupyterLab Desktop release](https://github.com/jupyterlab/jupyterlab-desktop#installation) for your operating system.
2. On the workshop page, select **Download Notebook**.
3. Open the downloaded `.ipynb` file in JupyterLab Desktop.
4. Confirm that the notebook uses a Python 3 kernel (look for "Python 3" in the top right corner of the open notebook).
5. Follow any additional setup/configuration instructions included in the notebook.

### Local Python with Jupyter

Use this option if Jupyter is already installed in a local Python environment and you are already familiar with using Python and Jupyter.

1. Download the `.ipynb` file from the workshop page.
2. Activate the Python environment you want to use and make sure [Jupyter is installed](https://jupyter.org/install).
3. Start JupyterLab or Jupyter Notebook.
4. Open the downloaded notebook and select a Python 3 kernel to run it.
5. Follow any additional setup/configuration instructions included in the notebook.

## Visual Studio Code

[Visual Studio Code](https://code.visualstudio.com/) can open and run `.ipynb` files with the [Jupyter extension](https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=ms-toolsai.jupyter). You will also need to have a local Python environment with [Jupyter installed](https://jupyter.org/install).

1. Install Visual Studio Code, the Python extension, and the Jupyter extension.
2. Download the workshop notebook.
3. Open the `.ipynb` file in Visual Studio Code.
4. Select a Python environment with Jupyter installed.
5. Follow any additional setup/configuration instructions included in the notebook.

This option has the same local dependency requirements as the "Local Python Server with Jupyter" option.

## Running in the cloud

::: callout-warning
## Sensitive data and cloud services

Do not use a cloud notebook service with protected health information (PHI), personally identifiable information (PII), credentials, or a sensitive FHIR endpoint unless that service and account have been approved by your organization. Use a local environment with proper security/privacy approval when handling sensitive data.
:::

### Google Colab

[Google Colab](https://colab.research.google.com/) can open a generated notebook from the public GitHub mirror. A Google account is required to use a hosted runtime and save work.

Use the **Open in Colab** button on the notebook page. The corrected link for the FHIR Data Analysis notebook was verified to resolve successfully. If the button is unavailable, download the `.ipynb` file from the workshop page and import it with **File → Upload notebook**.

Opening the notebook does not guarantee that every cell will run. Complete execution still requires access to a compatible FHIR server containing the workshop data.

### Binder

[Binder](https://mybinder.org) is often used to run Jupyter notebooks in the cloud. However, it can sometimes be unreliable so a one-click button is not included on this website to avoid a bad experience for users who encounter errors on Binder.

----

## Technical details

### How the notebooks on this website are published

The editable workshop sources are Quarto `.qmd` files. During deployment, Quarto generates `.ipynb` files and publishes them as a static website to the `gh-pages` branch on GitHub. Tools that rely on GitHub URLs for opening notebooks therefore need to use the `gh-pages` branch rather than the default branch.

### FHIR server and workshop data

Notebooks may rely on a FHIR server to provide sample data. Running the notebook does not include a running copy of this server. See [Standing Up a FHIR Testing Server](../modules/synthea-test-server.qmd) for more information.
